title: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Redfield Equation: Completely-Positive Resummation of Non-Markovian Dynamics
abstract: The Redfield equation with time-dependent coefficients (or TCL2 equation) gives one of the simplest perturbative descriptions of open quantum system dynamics derived from a microscopic theory. Its status as an approximation is nevertheless subtle: while perturbation theory fixes the reduced dynamics order-by-order in the system-environment coupling, solving the Redfield equation yields a particular resummation that need not preserve complete positivity. Here we compare Redfield evolution with an exponentiated (Magnus) resummation of the same second-order perturbative map, which is completely positive and trace preserving (CPTP) for a broad class of physical conditions. We also construct a simple CPTP resolvent resummation, illustrating the non-uniqueness of resummations of the same perturbative map. The Redfield and Magnus prescriptions agree to second order but differ through time-ordering corrections at higher orders. We exhibit a weak-coupling criterion which guarantees that Redfield evolution, even when non-Markovian, remains close to a CPTP map. We illustrate the criterion in two examples, focusing on finite-dimensional (qubit) systems. Our results clarify when, and why, Redfield evolution can remain reliable even when it is highly non-Lindbladian.
summary: This paper rigorously compares different mathematical methods—Redfield, Magnus, and resolvent—used to approximate the dynamics of open quantum systems. It establishes a weak-coupling criterion to determine when the standard Redfield approximation remains physically valid by ensuring the resulting evolution map is completely positive. This clarifies the reliability of these approximations, especially in non-Markovian regimes.
main_problem: The paper compares various mathematical resummations (Redfield, Magnus, resolvent) of the same second-order perturbative map describing open quantum system dynamics.
main_result: It derives a weak-coupling criterion that determines when the Redfield evolution remains close to a physically consistent, Completely Positive Trace-Preserving (CPTP) map, even when non-Markovian.
method: The analysis involves comparing the formal structures of different perturbative expansions (Redfield vs. Magnus) and deriving necessary conditions for the resulting map to preserve complete positivity.
model_or_system: The study focuses on open quantum systems, using finite-dimensional (qubit) systems coupled to an environment (bath) to analyze the reduced dynamics.
key_observables: Complete Positivity (CPTP) of the reduced quantum channel, and the comparison between the Redfield and Magnus evolution operators.
important_parameters: The system-environment coupling strength ($\lambda$) and the order of the perturbative expansion ($O(\lambda^2)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the positivity property of the environmental correlator and that the dynamics can be approximated by a second-order perturbative map.
figures_summary: Not specified by the notes, but the comparison of different resummations (Redfield vs. Magnus) is central.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the Redfield, Magnus, and resolvent resummations, derives the weak-coupling criterion, and illustrates its application in finite-dimensional qubit systems.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant for AMO and open quantum systems, as it provides rigorous mathematical tools to assess the physical validity (positivity) of common, yet approximate, master equation derivations.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Evolution of the excited-state population for an initially maximally-mixed system qubit (140). We compare the exact evolution with second-order perturbation theory and the resolvent, Redfield, and Magnus resummations. The top panel shows a detuned example with Ω/ω = 3 and λ/ω = 0.1. The bottom panel shows a near resonance case Ω≃ω with Ω/ω = 1.055 and λ/ω = 0.03, in which even perturbation theory does a poor job at approximating the exact dynamics. The Redfield and Magnus resummations are nearly indistinguishable at this scale; they are compared more directly in Figure 2. Notice that the resolvent resum- mation remains CP but does a poor job at approximating the exact dynamics.

FIG. 2. Complete-positivity diagnostics for the Redfield map, evaluated for the same parameter choices as in Fig. 1. The top panel shows the detuned case, Ω/ω = 3 and λ/ω = 0.1, while the bottom panel shows the near-resonant case, Ω/ω = 1.055 and λ/ω = 0.03. The Redfield map re- mains CPTP only while all three quantities are non-negative. Small violations develop in the near-resonant example, even though the Redfield and Magnus population dynamics are nearly indistinguishable.
FIG. 3. Plot of the correlator E(t, s) from Eq. (172) for the choice Ω/γ = 4. Notice that the fall-off of the imaginary part is much slower than the real part, consistent with Eq. (174).

FIG. 4. Complete-positivity diagnostic ∆CP as a function of ωt for the Redfield map in three parameter regimes. The top panel varies λ/ω, with Ω/ω = 0 and γ/ω = 10 fixed. The middle panel varies λ/ω, with Ω= 0 and γ/ω = 0.1 fixed. The bottom panel varies Ω/ω, with λ/ω = 0.1 and γ/ω = 0.25 fixed. In each case, increasing the late-time value ϵMag is accompanied by increasing violations of complete positivity at late times.
